stories.title: Claude Sonnet 5
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5, positioned as an upgrade to the Sonnet line — the tier most developers actually ship with, sitting between Haiku and Opus on the cost/capability curve.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The Sonnet tier is where most production workloads live. It's the model that hits the sweet spot on API cost vs. output quality for anything beyond simple classification. An upgrade here matters more day-to-day than an Opus release — if the capability jump is real, it means better reasoning and instruction-following at the same price point developers are already budgeting for. The developer changelog (linked separately from the marketing post) is the place to check for concrete deltas: context window changes, tool use improvements, or updated benchmarks on coding and reasoning tasks.
stories.considerations: The excerpt here is thin — we're working from an announcement stub, not the actual changelog. The meaningful signal is in the 'What's new in Claude Sonnet 5' developer docs, not the press release. Before adjusting any production prompts or switching model versions, check whether the capability gains come with any behavioral shifts — new models in the Sonnet line have historically changed refusal patterns or output formatting in ways that break existing prompts. Regression-test before you migrate.

stories.title: AIEWF Daily Dispatch: Loops, Software Factories & Forward Deployed Engineers
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
AI Engineer World's Fair Day 2 surfaced three recurring themes across talks: agentic loops as a core architectural pattern, the 'software factory' framing for multi-agent systems, and the Forward Deployed Engineer role — a hybrid between sales engineer and AI builder embedded directly at customers. Open models also drew significant floor attention.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The 'loops' framing is a concrete shift in how practitioners are describing agent architecture — not pipelines, not chains, but iterative feedback cycles where the model checks its own output before passing it downstream. The software factory metaphor goes further: teams are starting to treat LLM agents as workers on an assembly line, with orchestration layers managing task routing, quality gates, and retries. For developers building today, this means the interesting engineering work is moving from prompt design to loop control logic — when to retry, when to escalate, when to halt. The Forward Deployed Engineer concept signals that companies selling AI infrastructure are finding that generic docs aren't enough; customers need someone who can build the first working loop inside their stack.
stories.considerations: The software factory framing sounds clean in a conference talk but the analogy breaks down fast in production — factory workers don't hallucinate or randomly reinterpret their job description mid-shift. The open question is whether 'loop engineering' becomes a durable skill or just a transitional pattern that disappears once models get reliable enough to not need babysitting. Worth watching whether the Forward Deployed Engineer role scales or just becomes expensive professional services with an AI rebrand.

stories.title: Ahmad Osman on why local AI is catching up
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Ahmad Osman, speaking at AIEWF workshops, argues local AI deployment is closing the gap with cloud-hosted models — across consumer hardware (laptops, phones) and enterprise on-premise infrastructure.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The practical implication is that the build-vs-API calculus is shifting. If local inference on commodity hardware is genuinely competitive on quality, the cost and latency math starts favoring on-device for a wider class of tasks — especially anything with data residency requirements, offline constraints, or high query volume where per-token pricing compounds fast. Developers who dismissed local models six months ago may need to re-benchmark.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The excerpt is thin on specifics — no benchmark numbers, no named models, no hardware configurations. 'Catching up fast' is doing a lot of work here. Local AI has been 'almost there' for two years running, and the gap to frontier models on complex reasoning tasks remains real. Worth reading the full episode before updating your stack decisions based on a conference talk summary.

stories.title: Forward Deployed Engineers and the future of software engineering
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Sierra's Natalie Meurer argues that the product engineer and forward deployed engineer roles are converging — the distinction between building software and deploying it directly for customers is collapsing as AI tooling compresses the gap between prototype and production.

↳ THE REAL STORY
Forward deployed engineers (FDEs) traditionally sat at the customer interface: they took a core product and bent it to fit a specific enterprise's workflows, data, and edge cases. Product engineers built the thing; FDEs made it work in the wild. The argument here is that AI-assisted development now lets a single engineer do both — write the feature and ship the customer-specific configuration — without the handoff. For teams building on top of AI platforms like Sierra, this means fewer specialists and more generalists who own the full loop from code to customer outcome. Practically: smaller teams, faster iteration cycles, and engineers who need to understand business context as much as they understand the stack.
stories.considerations: The catch is that 'convergence' often means one role absorbs the other's workload without absorbing its compensation or headcount. If a product engineer is now also expected to do enterprise deployment, customer discovery, and edge-case wrangling, that's a scope expansion dressed up as a career evolution. Worth watching whether this framing benefits engineers or primarily benefits companies looking to justify leaner go-to-market teams. The FDE role exists partly because enterprise customers are genuinely complex — compressing that complexity into a single generalist may work at Sierra's scale and customer profile, but won't generalize cleanly to regulated industries or large legacy integrations.

stories.title: shot-scraper 1.10
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
shot-scraper 1.10 ships a new `shot-scraper video storyboard.yml` command — a YAML-driven way to record video demos of browser automation sequences.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The practical angle here is agent observability: you can now have an AI agent document its own browser work as a video, driven by a storyboard config file. For anyone building or debugging web agents, this means you get a reproducible, shareable artifact of what the agent actually did — not just logs or screenshots. The YAML-first approach keeps it scriptable and CI-friendly, so dropping video capture into an automated pipeline becomes a one-liner rather than a custom ffmpeg wrapper.
stories.considerations: The interesting question is how much this depends on the storyboard being authored correctly upfront versus generated dynamically by the agent itself. If the agent writes the YAML as it works, you get genuine replay value. If a human has to pre-script the storyboard, it's closer to a fancy screenshot sequence than true agent recording. Simon's post suggests the agent-authored path is the intent — worth checking how well that holds up with non-deterministic agent runs where the storyboard and the actual execution diverge.
